```{r}
#| include: false
library(sp)
library(sf)
library(terra)
library(adehabitatHR)
library(adehabitatLT)
library(ctmm)
source("R/slide_helpers.R")
source("R/simulators.R")

cilla <- subset(read_buffalo(), id == "Cilla")
xy  <- as.matrix(cilla[, c("x", "y")])
pts <- SpatialPoints(xy)

# 95% contour of an adehabitatHR UD, drawn with sf so holes stay holes
draw_contour <- function(ud, p, ...) {
  plot(st_geometry(st_as_sf(getverticeshr(ud, percent = p))), add = TRUE, ...)
}
blank_map <- function(main, xlim = range(xy[, 1]), ylim = range(xy[, 2])) {
  plot(NA, xlim = xlim, ylim = ylim, asp = 1, axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "", main = main)
}

mcp95   <- mcp(pts, percent = 95)
kd_href <- kernelUD(pts, h = "href", grid = 300, extent = 1)
kd_lscv <- suppressWarnings(kernelUD(pts, h = "LSCV", grid = 300, extent = 1))
lim95   <- bbox(getverticeshr(kd_href, percent = 95))
xl <- range(lim95[1, ], xy[, 1]); yl <- range(lim95[2, ], xy[, 2])
```

## Today

::: {.paradigm}
[Internal state]{.pbox}
[Motion capacity]{.pbox}
[Navigation capacity]{.pbox .on}
[External factors]{.pbox .on}
[Movement path]{.pbox .path .on}
:::

A home range is what a path looks like when **memory** (navigation) and the
**distribution of resources** (external factors) keep an animal in one place.
Today: how to estimate it — and when it does not exist.

---

## Where we are going

::: {.objectives}
1. From territorial polygons to probabilistic **utilisation distributions**
2. MCP, and why it is still reported
3. Kernel density estimation, and its sensitivity to bandwidth
4. Autocorrelation: from nuisance (Brownian bridges) to information (AKDE)
5. When a home range is a valid concept: stationarity and the occupation
   timescale
:::

. . .

::: {.keyidea}
Today's real learning objective is the comparison: four estimators, one
animal, four different answers — and a simulated animal whose true answer we
know.
:::

# 1 · What is a home range? {background-color="#14525a"}

---

## Burt's definition

> "That area traversed by the individual in its normal activities of food
> gathering, mating and caring for young."
> — Burt (1943)

. . .

::: {.incremental}
- Note what it **excludes**: exploratory forays, migration, dispersal
- Note what it does **not** say: nothing about probability, nothing about 95%
- Powell & Mitchell (2012): a home range is the part of its **cognitive map**
  an animal chooses to keep up to date — our estimators are crude proxies
:::

---

## From polygons to distributions

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| fig-align: center
px <- as(kd_href, "SpatialPixelsDataFrame")
ud <- rast(data.frame(coordinates(px), ud = px$ud), type = "xyz")
ud[ud < 0.02 * global(ud, "max")[[1]]] <- NA

par(mfrow = c(1, 2)); map_par()
blank_map("Polygon: inside or outside", xl, yl)
plot(st_geometry(st_as_sf(mcp95)), add = TRUE, col = adjustcolor(teal, 0.35), border = teal, lwd = 3)
points(xy, pch = 16, cex = 0.3, col = adjustcolor(ink, 0.3))
scale_bar(5)
blank_map("Utilisation distribution: how much time, where", xl, yl)
image(ud, col = hcl.colors(60, "YlGnBu", rev = TRUE), add = TRUE)
draw_contour(kd_href, 50, border = ink, lwd = 2.5)
draw_contour(kd_href, 95, border = ink, lwd = 2.5, lty = 2)
legend("bottomright", c("50%", "95%"), lty = c(1, 2), lwd = 2.5, bty = "n", cex = 1.4)
```

[Figure produced with own R code · data: Kruger buffalo, Getz et al. (Movebank)]{.credit}


The same buffalo, Cilla. On the left every part of the area counts the same;
on the right, core areas and rarely used edges are distinguished.

. . .

::: {.keyidea}
The UD is the object; "the home range" is a contour you draw on it. Say which
contour, and which estimator produced the UD.
:::

# 2 · Minimum convex polygon {background-color="#14525a"}

---

## MCP

The smallest convex polygon containing $x$% of the fixes.

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**For**

- Trivial to compute and explain
- Comparable with a century of literature
- No smoothing parameter to argue about
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Against**

- **Convex** — includes land never used
- Sensitive to outliers and sample size
- Area depends on how long you tracked
- No density information
:::
:::

. . .

Report it for comparability with old studies. Never as your only estimate.

---

## MCP on a real buffalo

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 4.8
#| fig-align: center
a95  <- mcp.area(pts, percent = 95,  unout = "km2", plotit = FALSE)[[1]]
a100 <- mcp.area(pts, percent = 100, unout = "km2", plotit = FALSE)[[1]]
days <- as.numeric(difftime(cilla$t, cilla$t[1], units = "days"))
dd   <- seq(5, floor(max(days)), by = 5)
grow <- sapply(dd, function(k)
  mcp.area(SpatialPoints(xy[days <= k, ]), percent = 95, unout = "km2", plotit = FALSE)[[1]])

layout(matrix(1:2, 1), widths = c(1, 1.25))
map_par()
blank_map(sprintf("MCP 95%%: %.0f km²   (100%%: %.0f km²)", a95, a100))
plot(st_geometry(st_as_sf(mcp(pts, percent = 100))), add = TRUE, border = ink, lty = 2, lwd = 2)
plot(st_geometry(st_as_sf(mcp95)), add = TRUE, col = adjustcolor(teal, 0.15), border = teal, lwd = 3)
points(xy, pch = 16, cex = 0.35, col = adjustcolor(ink, 0.35))
scale_bar(5)
slide_par()
plot(dd, grow, type = "o", pch = 16, lwd = 3, col = teal, ylim = c(0, max(grow) * 1.05),
     xlab = "Days tracked", ylab = "MCP 95% (km²)", main = "Area depends on duration")
```

[Figure produced with own R code · data: Kruger buffalo, Getz et al. (Movebank)]{.credit}


Left: the 95% MCP (solid) and 100% MCP (dashed) contain large stretches the
animal hardly used. Right: the same estimate from the first 5, 10, 15… days.

# 3 · Kernel density estimation {background-color="#14525a"}

---

## KDE

Put a small bump (kernel) on each fix and sum them into a **utilisation
distribution** (Worton 1989).

::: {.incremental}
- Gives a **density**: core areas, disjoint patches, used and unused parts
- The answer is dominated by the **bandwidth** $h$
  - $h_\text{ref}$ — optimal if the UD were a single bivariate normal; usually
    **over-smooths** real, multi-modal ranges
  - $h_\text{LSCV}$ — least-squares cross-validation; often **under-smooths**
    into fragments, and frequently **fails to converge**
:::

---

## How a kernel works

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| fig-align: center
set.seed(4)
x0 <- c(rnorm(6, 3, 0.8), rnorm(4, 7.5, 0.5))
g  <- seq(-1, 11, length.out = 500)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2)); slide_par()
for (h in c(0.25, 1.2)) {
  bumps <- sapply(x0, function(m) dnorm(g, m, h) / length(x0))
  plot(g, rowSums(bumps), type = "n", ylim = c(0, max(rowSums(bumps)) * 1.08), yaxt = "n",
       xlab = "Position", ylab = "Density", main = sprintf("bandwidth h = %s", h))
  matlines(g, bumps, lty = 1, col = adjustcolor(teal, 0.6), lwd = 1.5)
  lines(g, rowSums(bumps), lwd = 4, col = rust)
  rug(x0, lwd = 3, ticksize = 0.06, col = ink)
}
```

[Figure produced with own R code · simulated data]{.credit}


Ten fixes (ticks) in one dimension. Each gets a bump (thin lines); their sum
(thick line) is the estimated UD. Same fixes, two bandwidths, two stories.

---

## Same buffalo, two bandwidths

The buffalo Cilla, hourly fixes over 5 months, 95% contours:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 4.4
#| fig-align: center
par(mfrow = c(1, 2)); map_par()
for (k in list(list(kd_href, "h_ref = %.1f km: %.0f km²"),
               list(kd_lscv, "h_LSCV = %.1f km: %.0f km², did not converge"))) {
  a <- kernel.area(k[[1]], percent = 95, unout = "km2")[[1]]
  blank_map(sprintf(k[[2]], k[[1]]@h$h / 1000, a), xl, yl)
  draw_contour(k[[1]], 95, col = adjustcolor(teal, 0.35), border = teal, lwd = 2)
  points(xy, pch = 16, cex = 0.25, col = adjustcolor(ink, 0.3))
}
scale_bar(5)
```

[Figure produced with own R code · data: Kruger buffalo, Getz et al. (Movebank)]{.credit}


. . .

::: {.keyidea}
A factor of three from one analyst's choice. Report the bandwidth selector —
and check whether LSCV actually converged. `adehabitatHR` warns you; papers
rarely do.
:::

---

## Quiz

::: {.quiz}
You compute a 95% KDE with LSCV and get a range three times smaller than with
$h_\text{ref}$, made of dozens of small islands. `kernelUD()` printed "the
algorithm did not converge". What do you report?

- [ ] The LSCV result — it is data-driven and $h_\text{ref}$ is known to over-smooth
- [ ] The average of the two
- [x] That the KDE area is not well determined by these data, and prefer an estimator that accounts for autocorrelation
- [ ] The $h_\text{ref}$ result, because it converged

::: {.quiz-feedback}
LSCV fails in a characteristic way on GPS data: with many autocorrelated fixes
it chooses a tiny bandwidth that treats every cluster of consecutive fixes as a
separate hotspot. A non-converged bandwidth is not a result.

$h_\text{ref}$ "converges" only because it is a formula — it assumes a
unimodal range and has no way to be wrong in public. Neither is trustworthy
here. The disagreement itself is the finding: these data do not pin down a
KDE area, which points to the autocorrelation-aware methods on the next slides.
:::
:::

# 4 · Autocorrelation {background-color="#14525a"}

---

## The problem classical KDE has with GPS

Classical KDE assumes fixes are **independent** draws from the UD.

. . .

Hourly GPS fixes are nothing of the sort — the animal was 300 m away an hour
ago and will be 300 m away in an hour.

::: {.incremental}
- The **effective** sample size is far smaller than $n$
- The UD comes out **too narrow** — the range is under-estimated
- Collecting more fixes at a higher rate makes it **worse**, not better
:::

. . .

::: {.keyidea}
This is why area estimates from 1990s VHF studies (a few dozen fixes, days
apart) and modern GPS studies (thousands, an hour apart) are not comparable.
:::

---

## Same number of fixes, different information

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| cache: true
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 4.8
#| fig-align: center
set.seed(5)
long    <- do.call(simulate_bcrw, c(list(n = 60000), truth_rule))   # 20-min steps
true_ud <- kernelUD(SpatialPoints(long[seq(1, 60000, by = 10), c("x", "y")]), h = "href", grid = 200)
lim <- range(long$x, long$y)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2)); map_par()
for (k in list(list(long[20001:21000, ], "1,000 fixes, every 20 min (2 weeks)"),
               list(long[seq(1, 60000, length.out = 1000), ], "1,000 fixes, every 20 h (2.3 years)"))) {
  blank_map(k[[2]], lim, lim)
  draw_contour(true_ud, 95, border = rust, lwd = 3, lty = 2)
  est <- kernelUD(SpatialPoints(k[[1]][, c("x", "y")]), h = "href", grid = 200)
  draw_contour(est, 95, col = adjustcolor(teal, 0.25), border = teal, lwd = 2.5)
  points(k[[1]]$x, k[[1]]$y, pch = 16, cex = 0.4, col = adjustcolor(ink, 0.5))
  if (k[[2]] == "1,000 fixes, every 20 min (2 weeks)")
    legend("bottomright", c("true 95% range", "KDE 95%"), col = c(rust, teal),
           lty = c(2, 1), lwd = 3, bty = "n", cex = 1.3)
}
```

[Figure produced with own R code · simulated data]{.credit}


The central-place animal from Session 5, whose true range (dashed) we know.
Two weeks of dense fixes describe two weeks of the animal, not its range.

---

## Brownian bridges: use the path

Horne et al. (2007): between two consecutive fixes the animal was *somewhere*
on a random bridge connecting them.

::: {.incremental}
- The uncertainty of the bridge **grows with the time gap** and shrinks near
  each fix, scaled by a mobility parameter estimated from the data
- Uses the order of the fixes, not just their positions
- Handles **irregular sampling** naturally
- Answers a specific question: **where was the animal during the tracking
  period?** — its *occurrence* distribution
:::

. . .

::: {.keyidea}
A Brownian bridge maps where the animal **went**, not where it **could go**. It
shrinks around the observed path, so it is usually the smallest of the
estimates — correctly so, for the question it answers.
:::

---

## Autocorrelation is information

Fleming et al. (2015): stop treating autocorrelation as a nuisance.

::: {.incremental}
1. Fit a **continuous-time movement model** to the track (`ctmm`)
2. The model tells you how long the animal takes to cross its range — the
   **range-crossing time** $\tau_\text{position}$
3. From that, the **effective sample size**: roughly how many times the
   animal crossed its range during tracking
4. Weight the kernel accordingly: **AKDE**
:::

. . .

::: {.keyidea}
AKDE estimates the **range** distribution — where the animal would be found in
the long run — and gives it a **confidence interval**. If you track for three
range-crossing times, you effectively have three observations, however many
fixes you collected.
:::

---

## Where it went, where it lives

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| cache: true
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 4.8
#| fig-align: center
ltr <- as.ltraj(xy = as.data.frame(xy), date = cilla$t, id = "Cilla")
lik <- liker(ltr, sig2 = 30, rangesig1 = c(1, 100), plotit = FALSE)
bb  <- kernelbb(ltr, sig1 = lik$Cilla$sig1, sig2 = 30, grid = 300, extent = 0.3)
a_bb <- kernel.area(bb, percent = 95, unout = "km2")[[1]]

tel <- as.telemetry(data.frame(timestamp = cilla$t, location.long = cilla$lon,
                               location.lat = cilla$lat, individual.local.identifier = "Cilla"),
                    timeformat = "auto")
fit <- ctmm.select(tel, ctmm.guess(tel, interactive = FALSE))
ak  <- akde(tel, fit)
ci  <- summary(ak, units = FALSE)$CI / 1e6
ak_sf <- st_transform(as.sf(ak, level.UD = 0.95), 32736)
bx <- st_bbox(ak_sf)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2)); map_par()
blank_map(sprintf("Brownian bridge: %.0f km²", a_bb), bx[c(1, 3)], bx[c(2, 4)])
draw_contour(bb, 95, col = adjustcolor(gold, 0.3), border = gold, lwd = 2)
lines(xy, col = adjustcolor(ink, 0.4), lwd = 0.6)
scale_bar(5)
blank_map(sprintf("AKDE: %.0f km² (95%% CI %.0f–%.0f)", ci[2], ci[1], ci[3]), bx[c(1, 3)], bx[c(2, 4)])
plot(st_geometry(ak_sf[grepl("est", ak_sf$name), ]), add = TRUE,
     col = adjustcolor(rust, 0.25), border = rust, lwd = 3)
plot(st_geometry(ak_sf[!grepl("est", ak_sf$name), ]), add = TRUE, border = rust, lwd = 1.5, lty = 2)
points(xy, pch = 16, cex = 0.25, col = adjustcolor(ink, 0.3))
```

[Figure produced with own R code · data: Kruger buffalo, Getz et al. (Movebank)]{.credit}


Cilla again, on the same scale. The bridge hugs the path she travelled; AKDE
estimates the range she would use given time, with its confidence interval
(dashed).

---

## The variogram

The **semi-variance** as a function of time lag: how far apart, on average,
two positions $\Delta t$ apart are.

::: {.incremental}
- Rises at short lags as the animal moves away
- **Levels off** at an asymptote if the animal is range-resident: beyond the
  range-crossing time, positions are as far apart as they will ever be
- **Keeps rising** if the animal is not range-resident — drifting, dispersing,
  nomadic
- Proportional to the mean squared displacement of Session 5: the same curve,
  rescaled
:::

. . .

::: {.keyidea}
Look at the variogram **before** estimating any home range. No asymptote, no
home range.
:::

---

## Two variograms

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| cache: true
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| fig-align: center
data(gazelle)
gz     <- gazelle[[1]]
fit_gz <- ctmm.select(gz, ctmm.guess(gz, interactive = FALSE))

par(mfrow = c(1, 2)); slide_par(mar = c(6.2, 7, 3.2, 1), mgp = c(4.8, 0.8, 0))
plot(variogram(tel), CTMM = fit, fraction = 0.5, col.CTMM = rust, lwd = 3,
     main = "Buffalo Cilla: levels off")
plot(variogram(gz, dt = c(25, 259) %#% "hour"), CTMM = fit_gz, fraction = 0.65,
     col.CTMM = rust, lwd = 3, main = "Gazelle: no clear asymptote")
```

[Figure produced with own R code · data: Kruger buffalo, Getz et al. (Movebank); Mongolian gazelle, `ctmm` example data]{.credit}


Black: data. Red: fitted model. Cilla's range-crossing time is ~6 days, so her
3,500 fixes are worth ~19 independent ones. The gazelle's is ~5 months: two or
three crossings in a year.

---

## Quiz

::: {.quiz}
A Mongolian gazelle tracked for a year has an estimated range-crossing time of
~5 months (95% CI: 1 to 27 months), and its variogram shows no clear
asymptote. What should you conclude?

- [ ] Its home range is about 300,000 km², as AKDE reports
- [ ] You need more fixes per day
- [x] The animal is not demonstrably range-resident at the scale of the study; a home range is not a meaningful summary
- [ ] Switch to MCP, which does not need an asymptote

::: {.quiz-feedback}
These are the real `ctmm` results for a gazelle in the package's example data.
A range-crossing time whose upper bound exceeds the whole tracking period means
the animal crossed its "range" perhaps two or three times, or perhaps never:
the effective sample size is tiny and the area's confidence interval spans an
order of magnitude.

More fixes per day do not help: the constraint is **duration**, not frequency.
And switching to MCP hides the problem without solving it. Mongolian gazelles
are nomadic; for them, a home range may simply be the wrong concept.
:::
:::

# 5 · When is a home range valid? {background-color="#14525a"}

---

## Stationarity and the occupation timescale

::: {.incremental}
- Every estimator assumes the UD is **stationary** over the tracking period:
  the animal's space use is not systematically changing
- Seasonal shifts, dispersal and migration all violate it — segment first
  (Session 4) and estimate one range per stationary period
- The track must be much longer than the **range-crossing time**, or the
  animal has not yet shown you its range
- In Session 5, a buffalo tracked for 36 days was indistinguishable from a
  random walker; one tracked for 157 days was clearly confined
:::

. . .

::: {.keyidea}
"Must the time series be stationary?" Yes — over the timescale you summarise.
A home range is always a home range *for a stated period*.
:::

---

## Choosing an estimator

| | Answers | Use when | Watch out for |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| **MCP** | outer boundary | comparing to old literature | convexity, outliers, sample size |
| **KDE** | density of fixes | many roughly independent fixes | bandwidth; autocorrelation |
| **BBMM** | where it *went* | the path matters; irregular data | not a long-run range |
| **AKDE** | where it *lives* | modern GPS data: the default | needs range residency |

. . .

::: {.keyidea}
And before any of them: should you be estimating a home range at all? Check
the variogram, and check that the track is stationary.
:::

---

## Quiz

::: {.quiz}
For one buffalo you get 95% areas of: MCP 274 km², KDE ($h_\text{ref}$)
290 km², Brownian bridge 110 km², AKDE 400 km². Which statement is correct?

- [ ] AKDE is wrong because it disagrees with the others
- [ ] The Brownian bridge is wrong because it is the smallest
- [x] BBMM and AKDE answer different questions — where it went versus where it lives
- [ ] The average, 269 km², is the best estimate

::: {.quiz-feedback}
These are the real values for the buffalo Cilla. The Brownian bridge estimates
the **occurrence** distribution — the area around the path actually travelled
during tracking — so it hugs the path. AKDE estimates the **range**
distribution — where the animal would be found in the long run — and inflates
the area to account for the parts of the range the animal would visit given
more time.

Averaging estimates of different quantities produces a number that answers no
question. Choose the estimator from the question, and state the question.
:::
:::

## Today's practical

::: {.objectives}
**[→ Session 6 practical](exercise.qmd)**

1. MCP, KDE ($h_\text{ref}$ and LSCV), Brownian bridge and AKDE for one buffalo
2. Map all four; write one paragraph on why they differ
3. Variograms: a resident buffalo versus a nomadic gazelle
4. Ground truth: estimate the home range of the simulated animal from
   Session 5, whose true range we know — and see how each estimator fails
:::

---

## Recap

::: {.incremental}
- The UD is the object; a home range is a contour on it
- MCP for comparability only; KDE depends on bandwidth and ignores
  autocorrelation
- Brownian bridges map **occurrence**; AKDE estimates the **range** with a CI
- Autocorrelation is information: effective sample size = range crossings
- Check the variogram and stationarity **first**
:::
